[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is characterized by a *6-month progressive cognitive–behavioral syndrome* (i.e., insidious, subcortical-frontal–limbic pattern: forgetfulness, disorientation, executive dysfunction, paranoia, agitation) — consistent with early neurodegenerative or diffuse white matter pathology — followed by *acute-on-subacute right leg weakness and gait instability over 1 week*, indicating a new focal neurological deficit. Crucially, the brain MRI shows *disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect*, which strongly argues against acute inflammation (e.g., active MS plaques typically enhance when active), tumors, abscesses, or vasogenic edema. The absence of enhancement, meningeal signs, cranial nerve involvement, tremor, or speech/swallowing deficits makes primary gray-matter-predominant neurodegeneration (e.g., typical Alzheimer’s or FTD) less likely — those usually show cortical atrophy and hypometabolism on FDG-PET but *not* disseminated white matter lesions. Prion disease (e.g., sporadic CJD) is also unlikely: it typically presents with rapidly progressive dementia (<3 months), myoclonus, periodic EEG activity, and DWI/FLAIR cortical or basal ganglia hyperintensities — none of which are present; the 6-month tempo is too slow, and MRI shows white matter—not cortical—abnormalities.

The MRI pattern — disseminated, nonenhancing, nonmass-effect white matter lesions — is classic for *chronic, non-inflammatory, non-ischemic leukoencephalopathy*. Among the differential, hereditary small vessel diseases (e.g., CADASIL) often present with migraines, mood disturbances, and stepwise or insidious cognitive decline, but they typically show *symmetric anterior temporal pole and external capsule hyperintensities* on MRI — not “disseminated” lesions — and lack acute monoparesis. Metabolic causes (e.g., B12 deficiency) can cause subacute combined degeneration and white matter changes, but spinal cord involvement (dorsal column, corticospinal tract) would be expected to dominate — yet the patient has *right leg weakness* (suggesting unilateral corticospinal tract or motor cortex involvement), not symmetric sensory ataxia or Lhermitte sign; moreover, B12 deficiency rarely causes *disseminated* white matter lesions without spinal cord signal change.

The most compelling fit is *chronic autoimmune encephalomyelitis with predominant white matter involvement*, particularly **MOG antibody–associated disease (MOGAD)** in its *chronic relapsing or monophasic encephalomyelitis phenotype*. MOGAD can present with insidious cognitive-behavioral symptoms due to extensive white matter and deep gray matter (e.g., thalamic, basal ganglia) involvement — especially in adults with ADEM-like or “leukoencephalitis” presentations. Critically, MOGAD lesions are characteristically *nonenhancing* on MRI once subacute/chronic, and may be *disseminated* across hemispheres and lobes — unlike MS, which tends toward periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal lesions with frequent enhancement in active phases. MOGAD also commonly spares the spinal cord in some phenotypes (explaining why spinal MRI is pending but not yet abnormal), and can cause acute/subacute focal deficits (e.g., leg weakness) due to large, tumefactive or confluent white matter lesions affecting motor tracts. Importantly, anti-MOG testing is pending — and MOGAD is *serum-positive in >90% of cases*, with CSF often showing mild pleocytosis or normal findings (unlike MS or NMOSD), aligning with the absence of inflammatory CSF data so far. Anti-AQP4 is less likely: NMOSD typically causes severe optic neuritis or longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis — neither reported — and its brain lesions (e.g., area postrema) are usually enhancing and symptomatic (nausea/vomiting), not silent or cognitive-predominant.

Thus, while neurodegenerative and metabolic etiologies remain possible, the *combination of subacute cognitive-behavioral decline + acute focal motor deficit + disseminated nonenhancing white matter lesions* is highly characteristic of an immune-mediated *leukoencephalitis*, with MOGAD being the most probable diagnosis among the listed options — especially given the pending anti-MOG test and the MRI signature.

- 6-month progressive cognitive–behavioral syndrome (forgetfulness, disorientation, executive dysfunction, paranoia, agitation)  
- New-onset right leg weakness and gait instability over the past week  
- Brain MRI shows disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect

- Pending anti-MOG testing — a key diagnostic test for MOGAD  
- Absence of typical NMOSD features (e.g., optic neuritis, myelitis, area postrema syndrome) makes anti-AQP4 less likely  
- Disseminated white matter lesions without enhancement favor chronic immune-mediated leukoencephalitis over acute MS or infectious/inflammatory mimics  

[GAPS]  
- Serum and CSF anti-MOG antibody status (critical for confirmation)  
- Spinal MRI results (to exclude concomitant myelitis — though absence would further support MOGAD’s white matter–predominant phenotype)  
- CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands): MOGAD typically shows normal or mildly elevated WBC/protein, without OCBs — distinguishing it from MS  
- Brain FDG-PET: may show frontal–subcortical hypometabolism correlating with lesion burden, supporting immune-mediated network disruption  
- Visual evoked potentials: could detect subclinical optic nerve involvement, supporting MOGAD even without overt optic neuritis  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
MOG antibody–associated disease (MOGAD)

- **Neurodegenerative disorders with white matter involvement**: e.g., early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (especially posterior cortical or limbic variants), frontotemporal dementia (FTD) with white matter changes, or prion disease (though rapid progression and lack of myoclonus/confusion make this less likely).  
- **Metabolic/toxic encephalopathy**: But no systemic symptoms or exposure history reported; labs pending.  
- **Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2)**: Typically presents with cognitive/psychiatric features + seizures or movement disorders — not reported here.  
- **Chronic small vessel disease**: Unlikely to cause prominent *disseminated* white matter lesions *plus* rapid motor decline and prominent behavioral/cognitive changes over 6 months.  
- **Atypical demyelination**: MOGAD or NMOSD usually show enhancing lesions or spinal cord involvement — neither present yet. AQP4/MOG antibodies pending.  
- **Vitamin B12 deficiency or syphilis**: Can cause subacute combined degeneration + cognitive changes — but MRI pattern (nonenhancing disseminated WM lesions) is atypical; labs pending.  
- **CADASIL or other hereditary arteriopathies**: Possible, but usually presents earlier and with migraine/stroke — no family history elicited.  

Critical next steps implied by testing ordered:  
- CSF analysis (to assess for inflammation, infection, or neurodegeneration markers like 14-3-3 or RT-QuIC if prion suspected).  
- Serum/CSF NfL (elevated in axonal injury — helps gauge disease activity across neurodegenerative, inflammatory, or ischemic conditions).  
- FDG-PET (to detect patterns of hypometabolism supporting neurodegenerative diagnosis — e.g., temporoparietal in AD, frontal in FTD).  
- Spinal MRI (to rule out concomitant myelopathy contributing to leg weakness).  
- VEP (to assess for subclinical optic nerve involvement).  

No evidence yet of stroke, tumor, acute infection, or classic MS.

[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Summary**:  
A patient presents with a 6-month progressive cognitive–behavioral syndrome (forgetfulness, disorientation, executive dysfunction, paranoia, agitation) and new-onset right leg weakness and gait instability over the past week. Neurological exam reveals no cranial nerve deficits, speech or swallowing abnormalities, tremor, or signs of meningeal irritation. Brain MRI demonstrates *disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect*, suggesting a diffuse, non-acute, non-inflammatory white matter pathology.  

**Pending Investigations**:  
- CSF analysis (cell count, glucose, protein, oligoclonal bands, IgG index)  
- Serum: B12, folate, TSH, RPR/TPPA  
- Autoantibodies: anti-MOG, anti-AQP4  
- EEG  
- Brain FDG-PET  
- Serum and CSF neurofilament light chain (NfL)  
- Spinal MRI (cervical/thoracic/lumbar, with contrast)  
- Visual evoked potentials (VEP)  

**Provisional Differential Diagnosis**:  
1. Neurodegenerative disorder (e.g., atypical Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, or prion disease)  
2. Chronic autoimmune or parainfectious encephalomyelitis with predominant white matter involvement  
3. Metabolic or toxic leukoencephalopathy (e.g., B12 deficiency, chronic nitrous oxide exposure — though unreported)  
4. Hereditary small vessel disease (e.g., CADASIL, COL4A1-related)  
5. Atypical demyelinating disorder (e.g., MOGAD or NMOSD with limited phenotype)  

Further diagnostic workup is ongoing to distinguish between neurodegenerative, immune-mediated, metabolic, and genetic etiologies.

The clinical presentation is characterized by a *6-month progressive cognitive–behavioral syndrome* (i.e., insidious, subcortical-frontal–limbic pattern: forgetfulness, disorientation, executive dysfunction, paranoia, agitation) — consistent with early neurodegenerative or diffuse white matter pathology — followed by *acute-on-subacute right leg weakness and gait instability over 1 week*, indicating a new focal neurological deficit. Crucially, the brain MRI shows *disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect*, which strongly argues against acute inflammation (e.g., active MS plaques typically enhance when active), tumors, abscesses, or vasogenic edema. The absence of enhancement, meningeal signs, cranial nerve involvement, tremor, or speech/swallowing deficits makes primary gray-matter-predominant neurodegeneration (e.g., typical Alzheimer’s or FTD) less likely — those usually show cortical atrophy and hypometabolism on FDG-PET but *not* disseminated white matter lesions. Prion disease (e.g., sporadic CJD) is also unlikely: it typically presents with rapidly progressive dementia (<3 months), myoclonus, periodic EEG activity, and DWI/FLAIR cortical or basal ganglia hyperintensities — none of which are present; the 6-month tempo is too slow, and MRI shows white matter—not cortical—abnormalities.

The MRI pattern — disseminated, nonenhancing, nonmass-effect white matter lesions — is classic for *chronic, non-inflammatory, non-ischemic leukoencephalopathy*. Among the differential, hereditary small vessel diseases (e.g., CADASIL) often present with migraines, mood disturbances, and stepwise or insidious cognitive decline, but they typically show *symmetric anterior temporal pole and external capsule hyperintensities* on MRI — not “disseminated” lesions — and lack acute monoparesis. Metabolic causes (e.g., B12 deficiency) can cause subacute combined degeneration and white matter changes, but spinal cord involvement (dorsal column, corticospinal tract) would be expected to dominate — yet the patient has *right leg weakness* (suggesting unilateral corticospinal tract or motor cortex involvement), not symmetric sensory ataxia or Lhermitte sign; moreover, B12 deficiency rarely causes *disseminated* white matter lesions without spinal cord signal change.

The most compelling fit is *chronic autoimmune encephalomyelitis with predominant white matter involvement*, particularly **MOG antibody–associated disease (MOGAD)** in its *chronic relapsing or monophasic encephalomyelitis phenotype*. MOGAD can present with insidious cognitive-behavioral symptoms due to extensive white matter and deep gray matter (e.g., thalamic, basal ganglia) involvement — especially in adults with ADEM-like or “leukoencephalitis” presentations. Critically, MOGAD lesions are characteristically *nonenhancing* on MRI once subacute/chronic, and may be *disseminated* across hemispheres and lobes — unlike MS, which tends toward periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal lesions with frequent enhancement in active phases. MOGAD also commonly spares the spinal cord in some phenotypes (explaining why spinal MRI is pending but not yet abnormal), and can cause acute/subacute focal deficits (e.g., leg weakness) due to large, tumefactive or confluent white matter lesions affecting motor tracts. Importantly, anti-MOG testing is pending — and MOGAD is *serum-positive in >90% of cases*, with CSF often showing mild pleocytosis or normal findings (unlike MS or NMOSD), aligning with the absence of inflammatory CSF data so far. Anti-AQP4 is less likely: NMOSD typically causes severe optic neuritis or longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis — neither reported — and its brain lesions (e.g., area postrema) are usually enhancing and symptomatic (nausea/vomiting), not silent or cognitive-predominant.

Thus, while neurodegenerative and metabolic etiologies remain possible, the *combination of subacute cognitive-behavioral decline + acute focal motor deficit + disseminated nonenhancing white matter lesions* is highly characteristic of an immune-mediated *leukoencephalitis*, with MOGAD being the most probable diagnosis among the listed options — especially given the pending anti-MOG test and the MRI signature.

- 6-month progressive cognitive–behavioral syndrome (forgetfulness, disorientation, executive dysfunction, paranoia, agitation)  
- New-onset right leg weakness and gait instability over the past week  
- Brain MRI shows disseminated, nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect  
- No cranial nerve deficits, no speech/swallowing abnormalities, no tremor, no meningeal signs

- Absence of typical NMOSD features (e.g., optic neuritis, myelitis, area postrema syndrome) makes anti-AQP4 less likely  
- Disseminated white matter lesions without enhancement favor chronic immune-mediated leukoencephalitis over acute MS or infectious/inflammatory mimics  

[GAPS]  
- Serum and CSF anti-MOG antibody status (critical for confirmation)  
- Spinal MRI results (to exclude concomitant myelitis — though absence would further support MOGAD’s white matter–predominant phenotype)

- Visual evoked potentials: could detect subclinical optic nerve involvement, supporting MOGAD even without overt optic neuritis  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
MOG antibody–associated disease (MOGAD)
